translationRepairs: Hence the great founders' strategists left enduring political lineages, their merit recognized alongside dynastic houses.
Thus, when Yi Yin and Lü Shang served as commanders, their descendants received states that endured alongside Shang and Zhou.
伊、呂 names Yi Yin and Lü Shang, while 之將 places them in the military-command context of the passage; the original paraphrase omitted both men and their descendants' states.
Therefore commanders like yiyin day and Lü Shang had descendants with states, standing alongside Shang and Zhou.
Therefore commanders like Yi Yin and Lü Shang had descendants with states, standing alongside Shang and Zhou.
The garbled literal 'yiyin day' is not a reading of 伊; correcting to Yi Yin restores the intended name alongside Lü Shang.
They proposed commutation schedules replacing some mutilations with hard labor terms;
They respectfully proposed that the statutes be fixed as follows: those liable to a punishment that left the body intact should serve as wall-building or grain-pounding convicts;

諸當完者，完為城旦舂 defines the intact (non-mutilating) 完 grade as wall-building and pounding labor; the idiomatic gloss wrongly frames this clause as replacing mutilations and omits the statute wording, while the proposed replacement matches the Chinese.
Your servants respectfully propose fixing statutes: those who should be castrated instead become wall-building and pounding labor convicts;
Your servants respectfully propose fixing the statutes as follows: those liable to the intact punishment shall serve as wall-building or grain-pounding convicts;
完 is the intact non-mutilating labor grade, not castration (宮); translating 諸當完者 as those who should be castrated is a factual error that the proposed replacement corrects.
Classical Zhou jurisprudence included multi-layered evidentiary and mitigation frameworks.
The offices of Zhou employed the procedures of the Five Hearings, Eight Deliberations, Three Inquiries, Three Pardons, and Three Amnesties.
周官有五聽、八議、三刺、三宥、三赦之法 enumerates five named procedural categories; the idiomatic paraphrase erases those names, and the proposed replacement restores them accurately.

Set this in statute: those over eighty, below eight, and pregnant women before weaning, as well as teachers and dwarf retainers who should be arrested, are to be held by summons rather than bound detention.'

Set this in statute: those over eighty, below eight, and pregnant women who have not yet given birth, as well as music masters and dwarfs who should be arrested, are to be held by summons rather than bound detention.'
孕者未乳 means pregnant women who have not yet given birth, not before weaning; 師 beside 朱儒 are music masters, not teachers in general. The proposed literal fixes both errors.

Across the mid- and late Western Han reigns, capital sentences still averaged about one execution per thousand-odd persons yearly, and severe non-capital punishments ran at more than triple that rate.

The Han way had now flourished for more than two hundred years. Across the six reigns of Emperor Zhao, Emperor Xuan, Emperor Yuan, Emperor Cheng, Emperor Ai, and Emperor Ping, capital cases ending in death averaged a little more than one person in every thousand each year; sentences ranging from shaving punishment to amputation of the right foot were more than three times as numerous.

The Chinese names the six emperors and distinguishes capital cases from the range of lesser punishments beginning with 耐 and extending through right-foot amputation; the proposal mistranslated 耐 as exile.
In early Eastern Han recovery, social conditions resembled early Han: pro-weak governance and reduced private coercive power.

From the Jianwu through Yongping eras, the people had only recently emerged from the disasters of war and were mindful of preserving life, as in the time of Emperor Gaozu and Emperor Hui. Government policy restrained the strong and supported the weak; at court no minister privately wielded the power to inspire fear or grant favors, and in the localities there were no domineering magnates.

The Chinese compares Jianwu and Yongping conditions to the time of Gaozu and Emperor Hui and details the policy of restraining the strong, supporting the weak, and curbing private power; the revision restores those specifics in natural English.
Per capita criminal adjudication fell dramatically versus late Western Han, indicating relative legal clarity.
On a per capita basis, adjudicated criminal cases were less than two-tenths as numerous as during the reigns of Emperor Cheng and Emperor Ai; the administration could be called clear.
少於成、哀之間什八 means that the number was lower by eight-tenths, hence less than two-tenths of the Cheng-Ai level; the revision states the comparison clearly.
He reinterprets historical shifts as responses to declining social-moral conditions.

Xunzi, having made this argument, went on to reason from the conventional account: Yu succeeded Yao and Shun but, believing that moral virtue had declined, instituted mutilating punishments; Tang and King Wu retained them because customs were less refined than in the age of Yao and Shun.
The Chinese names Yu, Yao and Shun, Tang and King Wu, and the age of Yao and Shun; the revision restores the argument without the proposal's broken participial construction.
Given post-Zhou/Qin social deterioration, applying ultra-lenient antiquarian models is seen as impractical and dangerous.

Now Han has inherited the utter exhaustion left by declining Zhou and violent Qin. Customs are already less refined than under the Three Dynasties, yet to apply the punishments of Yao and Shun would be like trying to control a savage, bolting horse with a light bridle: it would run contrary to what the times require.

The Chinese names declining Zhou, violent Qin, the Three Dynasties, and the punishments of Yao and Shun, then compares them to controlling a fierce bolting horse with a light bridle; the revision restores every element clearly.

Set this in statute: those over eighty years old, those under eight, pregnant women who have not yet given birth, and masters or dwarfs who should be arrested and detained are to be detained by summons rather than kept in bonds.'

Set this in statute: those over eighty, those under eight, pregnant women who have not yet given birth, music masters, and dwarfs who must be arrested and detained shall be held under summons rather than in bonds.'
師 in this legal list means music masters; the revision also removes repetition and matches the literal field.

Now Han's way had reached flourishing for over two hundred years; examining the six reigns from Zhao, Xuan, Yuan, Cheng, Ai, and Ping, capital judgments averaged about one death sentence for every thousand-odd persons per year, while punishments from exile up to right-foot amputation were more than triple that rate.

The Han way had now flourished for more than two hundred years. Examining the six reigns of Zhao, Xuan, Yuan, Cheng, Ai, and Ping, capital cases ending in death averaged a little more than one person in every thousand each year; punishments from shaving the beard through amputation of the right foot were more than three times as numerous.
耐 is a shaving punishment, not exile; the revision also clarifies the six-reign comparison.

Xunzi having said this, further arguing from common opinion: Yu inherited after Yao-Shun and because his virtue had declined made corporal punishments; Tang and Wu followed because customs were thinner than Tang-Yu.

Xunzi's words being so, he further reasoned from the conventional account: Yu succeeded Yao and Shun, but believing virtue had declined, instituted mutilating punishments; Tang and Wu continued them because customs were less refined than in the age of Yao and Shun.
The revision restores the argument's subjects and chronology in grammatical English.

Now Han inherits the exhausted flow of declining Zhou and violent Qin; customs are already thinner than Three Dynasties, yet practicing Yao-Shun punishments is like controlling a fierce horse with light tack-contrary to timely rescue.

Now Han inherits the utter exhaustion left by declining Zhou and violent Qin. Customs are already less refined than under the Three Dynasties, yet applying the punishments of Yao and Shun is like controlling a fierce, bolting horse with a light bridle, contrary to what the times require.
The revision preserves every historical comparison and renders the light-bridle analogy in grammatical English.
